title: Why Everything Got So Expensive (Ranked by Category)
note: EP090 — The Price Tag series (topic 80). scenes.narration: Since the year two thousand, a flat-screen TV got about ninety-five percent cheaper — while a year of college got nearly two hundred percent more expensive. We blame inflation for everything, but here's the secret: not everything inflated. Some things quietly collapsed in price while others exploded. Today we rank what got wildly more expensive, what got cheaper, and the single rule that explains the whole bizarre split.

Here's the contrast that breaks the inflation story. The price of a college education has risen roughly two hundred percent this century. Over the same years, televisions, toys, and gadgets fell so far they're almost free. Same economy, same decades — and prices sprinting in opposite directions depending entirely on what you were buying.

So today we unpack the most important economic chart you've never seen. We'll rank the categories that exploded, the ones that cratered, reveal the one rule that explains which is which, expose the subsidy trap behind the risers, and show how to budget and invest around it. Because once you see the pattern, you can never unsee why everything feels so expensive.

scenes.memeBottom: the things made of human time are — gadgets got cheaper
scenes.narration: This is the upgrade your brain needs. 'Everything costs more' is the beginner take. The truth is far stranger and far more useful. Before we rank anything, let's agree on how prices are even measured.
First, how we measure the price of everything.
scenes.heading: The Great Divergence

scenes.narration: We track prices with the consumer price index — calculated as the weighted average price of a market basket of consumer goods and services. It bundles everything a typical household buys into one number. The problem is that a single average quietly hides a violent split, because the items inside that basket are moving in completely opposite directions.

And the basket itself is a quiet battleground. Which items go in, and how they're weighted, changes the headline inflation number governments report. Critics argue the official basket understates the true squeeze, because it leans on the things that got cheaper and underweights the essentials that exploded. The number you're told rarely matches the number you feel.

And inflation itself is just an increase in the average price of goods and services in terms of money. The word average is doing enormous, misleading work. The overall rate might read a tame two or three percent a year, while underneath it one category doubles and another gets cut in half. The headline number is a blur hiding a battle.

And this is why two people can argue about inflation and both be right. The person who just bought a laptop and a new wardrobe feels like prices are falling. The person paying tuition, rent, and a hospital bill feels robbed. They're living in the same economy, shopping in different halves of the same basket. The average they share describes neither of them.

So the real story isn't the average — it's the spread. Some prices rocketed up far faster than inflation, while others fell for decades straight. When you pull them apart and line them up, a startlingly clean pattern appears. And that pattern explains why your paycheck feels squeezed even when inflation looks low.

And the spread has a name worth knowing: relative prices. Overall inflation tells you the average is drifting up, but relative prices tell you which things are winning and losing against that average. The entire modern cost-of-living story is really a story about relative prices quietly, permanently diverging.
Which brings us to the chart that explains the modern economy.
scenes.heading: The Chart of the Century

scenes.caption: since 2000: some prices soar, some collapse
scenes.narration: Here it is — sometimes called the chart of the century. Plot the price of everything since two thousand and the lines fan apart dramatically. Shooting upward: hospital care, college, childcare, and housing. Crashing downward: TVs, software, toys, phones, and clothing. One economy, one time period, and a fan of lines heading to opposite corners of the page.

And the fan of lines has been widening for decades without stopping. This isn't a blip from one bad year or one crisis — it's a steady, structural drift that's been running since before most workers today were born. Which means it's not about to reverse on its own. The split is the baseline, not the anomaly.

scenes.title: Price RISE since 2000 (%)
scenes.narration: First, the things that exploded. Hospital services, up well over two hundred percent. College tuition, close behind. Childcare and housing, each up more than a hundred. Even overall prices rose around seventy-five. These are the big, unavoidable pillars of a modern life — and every one of them outran your wages.

And notice these risers are the non-negotiables. You can skip a new phone, but you can't skip a place to live, getting sick, or caring for a child. That's what makes their rise so painful: they hit everyone, they can't be avoided, and they've climbed fastest precisely because demand for them never drops no matter the price.

scenes.title: How much CHEAPER since 2000 (%)
scenes.narration: Now the things that collapsed. Televisions, around ninety-five percent cheaper. Toys and software, down roughly seventy. Phones and cellphone service, down more than half. Clothing, modestly cheaper. The stuff we fill our homes with got dramatically more affordable — even as the roof over those homes did the exact opposite.

Put the full gap in one number. Between the fastest riser and the fastest faller, the price gap since two thousand is well over three hundred percentage points. Two products sitting in the same shopping cart have had completely opposite fates — one nearly tripled, the other nearly vanished.
scenes.sub: gap between the biggest riser and faller since 2000

scenes.narration: Stare at those two lists and the pattern jumps out. The things that got cheaper are gadgets, goods, physical products. The things that got brutally expensive are services — care, teaching, shelter, attention. The divide isn't random at all. It's the single most important line in the whole economy, and there's one rule that draws it.

scenes.memeBottom: goods got cheaper, human services got dearer
scenes.narration: Once you internalize this, the lazy explanation stops satisfying you. It isn't that money simply buys less across the board. It's that the economy quietly sorted every price into one of two buckets — and which bucket decided its entire fate.
So here is the rule that explains all of it.
scenes.heading: The One Rule

scenes.caption: things get cheaper; human time gets dearer
scenes.narration: The rule is this: anything you can manufacture, globalize, or automate gets cheaper over time. Anything made of irreplaceable human time gets more expensive. A TV can be built by robots in a cheaper country every year. A teacher, a nurse, a doctor, a daycare worker — their hours can't be shipped overseas or handed to a machine. One side of the economy scales. The other can't.

scenes.memeTop: a cheaper TV every single year
scenes.memeBottom: a doctor's visit you can actually afford
scenes.narration: This is the trade the modern economy quietly forced on us. Endless cheaper gadgets, or affordable essentials. We got the first button pressed over and over, and the second one taken away. Entertainment has never been cheaper; a stable life has rarely been dearer.

The cheap side runs on globalization — the process of increasing interdependence and integration among the economies of the world. Once a product could be made anywhere and shipped everywhere, competition and cheaper factories drove its price relentlessly down. Your electronics got cheaper because the entire planet was suddenly competing to build them.

And globalization didn't just lower prices — it capped them. The moment a product can be made anywhere, no single company can charge much more than the cheapest global producer. That ceiling is why gadget prices barely budge even now. Services never got that ceiling, because you can't import a haircut, a surgery, or a kindergarten teacher from across the world.

Add automation on top, and goods got even cheaper. Every year, factories make TVs, clothes, and toys with less human labor and more machinery. Productivity soars, costs fall, and the savings land in your lap as lower prices. For physical, tradable things, technology has been a relentless, decades-long discount machine.

And notice the quality twist. The cheap stuff didn't just get cheaper — it got better. Today's budget TV would humiliate a top-of-the-line model from two thousand. But a doctor's hour is still a doctor's hour, and a classroom is still a classroom. On one side, more for less. On the other, the same, for much more.

And the cheap side quietly subsidized the expensive side for years. Falling gadget and clothing prices held the overall inflation number down, masking how fast the essentials were climbing. For two decades, cheap imported goods let politicians and central banks claim inflation was tame — while rent, tuition, and healthcare quietly doubled underneath that comfortable average.

scenes.caption: why human-powered services keep rising
scenes.narration: But services are the opposite. A string quartet needs the same four musicians it did two centuries ago — you can't automate it. Yet those musicians' wages still rise to keep up with the rest of the economy. So the cost of anything made of human time climbs relentlessly, even without getting any better. Economists call this cost disease, and it quietly governs healthcare, education, and care.

The research is blunt about the result: in these labor-heavy fields, these sectors of the economy become more expensive over time, no matter what. There's no productivity miracle coming for a one-on-one doctor's visit or a classroom. So their prices rise, decade after decade, built into the very structure of how an economy works.

And cost disease sounds like a flaw, but it's partly a sign of success. Services feel expensive precisely because everything else got so productive and cheap. A rich economy can afford to pay teachers and nurses rising wages — the dear price of human care is, strangely, the price of broad prosperity. That doesn't make the bill easier to pay.

props.name: heart
props.label: we can afford to pay people

scenes.narration: But cost disease alone doesn't explain the worst offenders.
scenes.heading: The Subsidy Trap

scenes.narration: The true runaways — college, healthcare, housing — share a second accelerant: subsidized or financed demand. When governments guarantee student loans, when insurance hides the true price of care, when cheap mortgages flood housing, buyers can pay more, so sellers charge more. The help meant to make things affordable quietly pushes their prices even higher.

And the subsidy trap is a vicious loop. Prices rise, so the public demands more help affording them. The extra help lets buyers pay even more, so prices rise again, triggering calls for yet more aid. College and healthcare have been spinning this exact wheel for decades — each round of assistance quietly swallowed by the next price increase.

Here's the subsidy trap in one line. Decades of research link easy student loans directly to rising tuition: for every extra dollar of loan money made available, colleges captured a large share of it as higher prices. The aid didn't make college cheaper for students. It mostly made it more expensive for everyone.
scenes.sub: subsidized demand captured as higher prices

scenes.caption: the essentials soared; the extras got cheap
scenes.narration: And here's the cruel twist in one image. The categories that soared are the essentials — the things you must buy to build a stable life: a home, healthcare, a degree, childcare. The categories that got cheaper are the extras — the TVs, gadgets, and toys. Life's necessities inflated. Life's distractions went on sale. That's the squeeze, in a single picture.

And supply constraints pour fuel on the fire. Zoning laws throttle how many homes get built. Medical schools and licensing limit how many doctors exist. When demand is subsidized but supply is legally capped, prices don't just rise — they scream upward. The worst offenders are almost always the ones where we fuel buying and forbid building.

Measured properly, it's stark. Real value takes into account inflation and the value of an asset against what it can actually buy. In real terms, your television is nearly free — but your rent, your doctor, and your child's school each quietly cost twice what they did at the start of the century. You feel richer in stuff and poorer in life.

And this explains a generational mystery. Older relatives insist a single salary once bought a house, a family, and a comfortable life. They're not misremembering. Back then, the essentials were cheap and only the gadgets were dear. Today it's flipped — so the same salary buys a wall of cheap electronics but can't cover the life that used to come standard.

And this reframes the whole 'kids these days' debate. Young people aren't worse with money because they own nice phones and cheap clothes — those are the categories that collapsed in price. They're struggling because the things that signal a stable adult life, a home and a family, sit squarely on the side that exploded. The goalposts physically moved.
So what do you actually do about living inside this split?
scenes.heading: What To Do

scenes.narration: First, stop budgeting for the cheap stuff and start obsessing over the expensive stuff. The gadgets and clothes barely move your finances anymore. Housing, healthcare, education, and childcare are the entire game. Win on those four, and you win the decade. Agonizing over the price of a TV while overpaying on rent is fighting the wrong war entirely.

And protect yourself by buying the durable stuff when it's cheap and refusing to overpay for status versions of it. A modest phone, a used car, last year's model — the goods side rewards patience with ever-lower prices. Every dollar you don't waste proving status on cheap categories is a dollar freed up for the essentials that actually decide your future.

Second, get on the owning side of the things that inflate. If housing keeps rising, own a home instead of renting the increase. If a sector's prices climb forever, investing in it means the inflation works for you, not against you. The same forces squeezing you as a consumer can enrich you as an owner. Pick which side of the chart you're on.

And where you can, shift spending from the dear side to the cheap side on purpose. Stream entertainment instead of chasing status, but never cheap out on the leverage points — a home in the right place, your health, your skills. Starve the categories technology made cheap, and fund the ones that actually compound your life.

And turn the rule into an investing compass. The sectors with pricing power — the ones that can raise prices every year because demand never quits — are exactly the ones worth owning a piece of. Healthcare, essential housing, and the companies behind them ride the same wave that drowns you as a consumer. Own the tollbooths you're forced to pay.

Because here's the real lesson. The economy didn't get uniformly more expensive — it split in two. The things made by machines got cheaper, and the things made by people got dearer. And almost everything that actually matters for a good life sits on the expensive side. That's not bad luck. It's the deep structure of a modern economy, finally made visible.
